Finally, we discuss future research opportunities toward proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning could become an integral part of autonomous hardware design.

papers.title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
papers.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.

papers.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
papers.summary: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify

papers.title: Exploring Synchrony for Communication in Modular Neural Networks
papers.summary: One motivation for modular neural networks is to divide computation across components that learn distinct, reusable functions, which could then be recombined to support compositional generalisation. In practice, modular structure alone does not guarantee that such roles develop, and unrestricted communication between modules can undermine any specialisation that does emerge. This raises the question of how modular communication should be organised. The problem can be viewed as an analogue of the perceptual binding problem, where synchrony has been proposed as a mechanism for coordinating distributed representations. We introduce SyncNet, a modular architecture that separates module content from a dynamical phase state: learnt Kuramoto dynamics evolve the phases, while phase alignment determines communication through a shared channel. We evaluate SyncNet on Sort-of-CLEVR for relational reasoning and on SQOOP for systematic generalisation, where lower pair variety demands more recombination at test time. SyncNet gives the best held-out accuracy of the models compared at the three lowest pair varieties, by 5.1 percentage points at the hardest, and is competitive on Sort-of-CLEVR though below the strongest attention baselines. Test-time overrides show that performance depends on phases that evolve: fixed phases cost as much as no addressing at all, and permuting which module holds which region is nearly as damaging. A content-addressed variant trained from scratch nonetheless matches it, so the benefit appears to come from the modular decomposition rather than synchrony itself.

papers.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
papers.summary: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

papers.title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
papers.summary: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

papers.title: On Federated Averaging with Partial Participation under a General Variance Condition
papers.summary: In this paper, we study the convergence of Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with partial participation under a general variance condition. In each communication round, the server samples $S$ of the $n$ clients uniformly at random without replacement. The stochastic gradients are assumed to satisfy the so-called ABC condition, which allows their variance to grow with the local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a finite-time stationarity bound in terms of the heterogeneity measure $\sigma_f^\star:=f^\star-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^\star$ and the client sampling factor $I_S:=(n-S)/(n-1)$. Here, $f^\star$ and $f_i^\star$ denote the infima of the global average objective and client $i$'s local objective, respectively. The bound exhibits a linear speedup in the number of sampled clients $S$ and recovers the full-participation result when $S=n$. Under diminishing stepsizes, we further prove that the gradient norm converges to zero both in expectation and almost surely. Notably, compared with existing analyses of FedAvg with partial participation, our results require no additional data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD), and the sampling-induced term in our bound is not amplified by the number of local updates at the leading order. The importance of removing the BGD assumption is illustrated by an example that is smooth and lower bounded but violates BGD, yet is covered by our analysis.

papers.title: PSL-RGHA: Parallel Split Learning with Reference Gradient Half-Space Alignment for Mitigating Gradient Divergence
papers.summary: The escalating complexity of deep neural networks hinders the deployment of federated learning (FL) on resource-constrained devices, especially for multimedia applications such as on-device image classification and speech recognition. Parallel split learning (PSL) has emerged as a promising solution by offloading a substantial portion of the computational workload to the server through layer-wise model partitioning, making it particularly suitable for resource-limited visual and speech intelligence scenarios. However, the absence of client-side aggregation renders PSL sus ceptible to severe training divergence and potential convergence failure under heterogeneous data distributions. To address this challenge, we propose PSL-RGHA, a gradient-aligned PSL framework that employs reference gradient half-space alignment mechanism to mitigate training divergence among client devices. PSL-RGHA comprises two novel components: reference gradient progressive construction (RGPC) and gradient half-space alignment (GHA). Specifically, RGPC evaluates the directional consistency of client gradients and progressively synthesizes a robust reference gradient via Weiszfeld updates, effectively approximating the global descent direction. Then, GHA constrains client gradients within the reference half-space defined by RGPC to mitigate gradient conflicts and rectify local updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our PSL-RGHA framework outperforms existing baselines in various settings.

papers.title: Self-stabilization and Byzantine Tolerance for Maximal Independent Set
papers.summary: We analyze the impact of transient and Byzantine faults on the construction of a maximal independent set in a general network. We adapt the self-stabilizing algorithm presented by Turau for computing such a vertex set. Our algorithm is self-stabilizing and also works under the more difficult context of arbitrary Byzantine faults. Byzantine nodes can prevent nodes close to them from taking part in the independent set for an arbitrarily long time. We give boundaries to their impact by focusing on the set of all nodes excluding nodes at distance 1 or less from Byzantine nodes, and excluding some of the nodes at distance 2. As far as we know, we present the first algorithm tolerating both transient and Byzantine faults under the fair distributed daemon. We prove that this algorithm converges in $ \mathcal O(\Delta n)$ rounds w.h.p., where $n$ is the number of nodes and $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the network. Additionally, we present a modified version of this algorithm for anonymous systems under the adversarial distributed daemon that converges in $\mathcal O(n^{2})$ moves both in expected value and with high probability.

papers.title: fRAC: Remote Accelerator Calls on Hostless FPGAs
papers.summary: Hardware accelerators are essential for meeting microsecond-scale demands in distributed applications, but invoking them over the network remains bottlenecked by host software. Host-mediated paths (RPC, RDMA) still rely on the CPU to reassemble requests and launch accelerators, which dominates end-to-end latency, while packet-level offload on SmartNICs lacks any notion of a complete request. We introduce the Remote Accelerator Call (RAC) paradigm, in which transport ingestion, request reassembly, dispatch, and accelerator invocation are handled entirely in hardware. We build fRAC, a hostless prototype that implements this network-to-accelerator interface as a lightweight shim on an FPGA hosting multiple virtualized accelerators, reconfigurable at runtime in a few milliseconds. Serverless functions backed by fine-grained accelerators are a natural fit, since host-mediated invocation overhead can match or exceed their short execution times. fRAC achieves under 7.8us end-to-end latency while sustaining application throughput of up to 90 Gbps. Compared to highly optimized DPDK-based CPU and DPU baselines, it achieves at least 80% lower latency under saturation, while consuming 85% less power.

papers.title: Programmable GPU-Accelerated dApps for Real-Time Edge Inference and ISAC on NVIDIA Aerial Testbed
papers.summary: The transition of cellular networks to (i) software-based systems on commodity hardware and (ii) platforms for services beyond connectivity introduces critical system-level challenges. As sensing emerges as a key feature toward 6G standardization, supporting Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) with limited bandwidth and piggybacking on communication signals, while maintaining high reliability and performance, remains a fundamental challenge. In this paper, we provide two key contributions. First, we present a programmable, open-source framework for processing PHY signals through real-time, GPU-accelerated Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on the edge Radio Access Network (RAN) infrastructure. Building on the Open RAN dApp architecture, the framework interfaces with a GPU-accelerated gNB based on NVIDIA Aerial Testbed (ATB), feeding PHY data to custom AI logic with about 84 $\mu$s of framework latency per slot and control loops with inference in about 123 $\mu$s for lightweight TensorRT models, multiple inference engines, and support for several AI backends. We evaluate the framework on two GPU platforms, with different GPU sharing modes and an increasing number of cells and dApps. Second, we demonstrate the framework capabilities through cuSense, an indoor localization dApp that consumes uplink DMRS channel estimates, removes static multipath components, and runs a neural network to infer the position of a moving person. Evaluated on a 3GPP-compliant 5G NR deployment, cuSense achieves a mean localization error of 73 cm on runs unseen during training, with 79% of predictions falling within 1 meter, and runs live in 241 $\mu$s, without dedicated sensing hardware or modifications to the 5G signals. The framework is released as open source, together with the cuSense dataset, providing a reference design for future AI-native RANs and ISAC applications.

papers.title: For Generalised Algebraic Theories, Two Sorts Are Enough
papers.summary: Generalised algebraic theories (GATs) allow multiple sorts indexed over each other. Categories have two sorts, objects and morphisms, and the latter are double-indexed over the former. Martin-L\"of type theory has four sorts: contexts, substitutions, types and terms. For example, types are indexed over contexts, and terms are indexed over both contexts and types. In this paper we show that any GAT can be reduced to a GAT involving only two sorts: a first one without dependencies, and another one indexed over the former. We show that a model of the reduced GAT is equivalently given by a pair consisting of a model of the original GAT, which we call the core model, and a "cartesian" morphism from the family of sets induced by this core model. In a type-theoretic metatheory, the initial model of a GAT is called a quotient inductive-inductive type (QIIT). The above characterisation justifies soundness of the reduction, in the sense that the QIIT of the original GAT can be simulated from the QIIT of the reduced GAT, by taking its core model. A particular case of our reduction is the well-known method of reducing mutual inductive types to a single indexed family. Other instances of this reduction can be found in the literature to simulate sophisticated QIITs in Cubical Agda. Indeed, the reduced GAT is simpler than the original GAT in the following aspects: it does not have sort equalities; it does not have interleaved sorts and operations; if the original GAT did not have interleaved sorts and operations, then the reduced GAT won't have operations interleaved between different sorts. Our approach is semantic in that it does not rely on a syntactic description of GATs, but instead, on Uemura's bi-initial characterisation of the category of (finite) GATs in the 2-category of finitely complete categories with a chosen exponentiable morphism.

papers.title: SplitCom: Communication-efficient Split Federated Fine-tuning of LLMs via Temporal Compression
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning of on-device large language models (LLMs) mitigates privacy concerns by preventing raw data sharing. However, the intensive computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for resource-constrained edge devices. To overcome these limitations, split federated learning (SFL) emerges as a promising solution that partitions the model into lightweight client-side and compute-intensive server-side sub-models, thus offloading the primary training workload to a powerful server. Nevertheless, the high-dimensional activation exchanges in SFL lead to excessive communication overhead. To overcome this, we propose SplitCom, a communication-efficient SFL framework for LLMs that exploits temporal redundancy in activations across consecutive training epochs. Inspired by video compression, the core innovation of our framework lies in selective activation uploading only when a noticeable deviation from previous epochs occurs. To balance communication efficiency and learning performance, we introduce two adaptive threshold control schemes based on 1) bang-bang control or 2) deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG)-based reinforcement learning. Moreover, we implement dimensionality reduction techniques to alleviate client-side memory requirements. Furthermore, we extend SplitCom to the U-shape architecture, ensuring the server never accesses clients' labels. Extensive simulations and laboratory experiments demonstrate that SplitCom reduces uplink communication costs by up to 98.8\,\% in its standard configuration and total communication costs by up to 95.8\,\% in its U-shape variant without noticeably compromising model performance.

papers.title: KAIROS: Stateful, Context-Aware Power-Efficient Agentic Inference Serving
papers.summary: Power has become a central bottleneck for AI inference. This problem is becoming more urgent as agentic AI emerges as a major workload class, yet prior power-management techniques focus almost entirely on single-turn LLM serving. Our analysis shows that agentic serving behaves fundamentally differently: each request carries long-lived context that evolves across tool-interleaved turns, and lowering GPU frequency can push the system into a thrashing regime where memory pressure sharply worsens both performance and power efficiency. These observations show that power optimization for agentic serving requires rethinking. We present KAIROS, a context-aware power optimization system for agentic AI serving. KAIROS uses agent context as a first-class control signal to jointly manage GPU frequency, per-instance concurrency, and multi-instance request placement. This enables KAIROS to save power when memory headroom exists while avoiding thrashing and preserving performance targets. At a high level, KAIROS tracks requests at agent granularity, adapts local control to context growth and agent progress, and routes agents across instances to jointly improve power efficiency and memory stability. Evaluated across diverse software and data engineering agentic tasks, KAIROS achieves an average of 27% (up to 39.8%) power reduction while meeting the performance targets.

papers.title: RECURSUM: Automated Code Generation for Recurrence Relations Exceeds Expert Optimization via LayeredCodegen
papers.summary: Automated code generation can systematically exceed expert hand-optimization for recurrence relations--computational primitives ubiquitous in orthogonal polynomials, special functions, numerical integration, and molecular integral evaluation. We present RECURSUM, a Python DSL generating optimized C++ for arbitrary recurrence relations via three backends--template metaprogramming, a novel LayeredCodegen backend, and runtime loop-based evaluation--specifying recurrences in 10--30 lines of Python that generate 650+ lines of production C++. LayeredCodegen achieves 9.8$\times$ speedup over expert hand-written code and 1.9$\times$ over template metaprogramming for McMurchie-Davidson Hermite coefficients, through zero-copy output parameters, guaranteed inlining, and exact-sized stack buffers. A DAG-topological generalization of this architecture--built to express the four-center electron-repulsion integral that LayeredCodegen's tower model cannot--beats libint2, a mature, two-decade-refined production library, on 12 of 14 Cartesian integral classes, with $\sim$2$\times$ faster contracted Coulomb/exchange (J/K) matrix construction (alkanes and 3-D DNA fragments alike) and 1.1--2.7$\times$ faster one-electron integrals, completing the full Hartree-Fock integral set from one DAG framework. We validate 24 recurrence types spanning pure mathematics, numerical analysis, and quantum chemistry; production benchmarks confirm these speedups propagate to complete algorithms, matching expert baselines within 3.3\%. By eliminating the dual expertise barrier of domain knowledge and C++ metaprogramming, RECURSUM establishes systematic code generation--not hand-tuning--as the performance ceiling for recurrence algorithms.

papers.title: Bridge: Optimizing Collective Communication Schedules in Reconfigurable Networks with Reusable Subrings
papers.summary: Optical circuit-switched networks have emerged as an appealing alternative to electrical fabrics as they can reconfigure the network topology at runtime, reducing communication cost and improving bandwidth utilization. Yet exploiting optical reconfigurable networks for collective communication comes with a fundamental trade-off: each reconfiguration incurs non-negligible delay and the benefit of a new topology depends on future traffic. The central question is therefore when reconfiguration is worth its cost. While prior work has demonstrated the benefits of reconfiguration, the opportunity to reuse optical links to optimize multiple steps remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present Bridge, a reconfiguration strategy for frequently used collective communication primitives, namely All-to-All, AllReduce, Reduce-Scatter, and AllGather. Bridge exploits the structure of Bruck's communication pattern to support efficient sparse reconfiguration. The key idea is to reduce propagation and transmission delay by directly connecting immediate communication partners and preserve efficient reachability to future peers through connected subrings. As a result, optical links can be reused across multiple subsequent steps, allowing the benefit of reconfiguration to amortize beyond a single step. Our evaluation shows that Bridge reduces All-to-All completion time by typically 3x to 10x over static baselines and is effective even with millisecond-scale reconfiguration delays; for AllReduce up to 1.5x against existing reconfiguration strategies, and by 1.5x to 6.6x against the Ring algorithm on low to moderate-sized workloads.

papers.title: Revisiting Eigenvalue-Only Divide-and-Conquer Tridiagonal Eigensolver from Algorithmic Perspective
papers.summary: Divide-and-conquer (D&C) is the natural parallel strategy for symmetric tridiagonal eigenvalue decomposition, yet eigenvalue-only solvers fall back to serial QR algorithm because the quadratic transform state each merge carries exhausts memory at scale. In this paper, we demonstrate that each merge stage in D&C needs only two boundary rows, the first and last rows of a node's eigenvector block, and these close into a recurrence whose parent rows follow from its children's and local merge data alone, so the state is carried up the tree with nothing replayed and persistent memory drops from quadratic to linear. Because this state keeps no replay workspace, adapting the schedule to each merge's post-deflation active rank is a scheduling choice, so both CPU and GPU spend finer-grained parallelism only where substantial secular work survives. We evaluate optimized CPU and GPU implementations, with complexity and correctness analysis, against QR, bisection, and D&C routines in standard libraries.

papers.title: On the Solvability of Sound Distributed Verification under Byzantine Faults
papers.summary: Modern distributed systems, ranging from distributed tracing platforms to blockchain oracle networks, frequently rely on processes holding partial observations to collectively certify a global execution state. Under Byzantine failures, a single malicious process withholding or fabricating partial states renders sound verification impossible, as genuine observations remain indistinguishable from fabricated assertions. To overcome this impossibility, we study input overlap x: the minimum number of processes that initially witness each element of a target execution I. We formalize this challenge as the x-reconstruction problem in asynchronous message-passing systems with up to t failures, where the goal is for all correct processes to recover I completely given an input overlap x. We establish tight matching upper and lower bounds for solvability: under crash failures, x-reconstruction is solvable if and only if x >= t + 1; under Byzantine failures, x-reconstruction is solvable if and only if x >= 2t + 1. Finally, we connect these structural bounds to semantic verification. For globally dependent safety properties (such as consensus, linearizability, k-set agreement, and leader election), sound verification under Byzantine faults requires a certificate of size c = t + 1 to guarantee at least one honest report. Consequently, sound distributed verification under Byzantine faults is achievable if and only if the input overlap satisfies x >= 2t + 1.

papers.title: A Lightweight, Open-Source Network Digital Twin Blueprint for IoT-Edge Environments
papers.summary: IoT-Edge-Cloud infrastructures are increasingly heterogeneous, and experimenting across the continuum is difficult and risks disrupting live systems. Network Digital Twins (NDT) are a pragmatic answer, yet practitioners lack a structured account of three things: how to build an NDT from open tools, how to model wireless impairments, and how to understand whether the twin is faithful to the physical network, or not. This tutorial introduces NDT through the IRTF reference model and walks through a lightweight open-source blueprint built on Containerlab, Open vSwitch, \textit{Open Network Operating System (ONOS)}, and Prometheus/Grafana. It then explains how to define wireless impairment profiles (static, model-based, trace-driven, AI-generated, and live), and what each approach can and cannot reproduce. Finally, it presents a workflow to validate the twin against the physical network. A proof-of-concept Edge case study illustrates the procedure, including the pitfalls encountered and the lessons learned. Directions for future research are outlined.

papers.title: Reconciling Strict SLOs with Low Cost under Fine-Grained Load Fluctuations
papers.summary: Cloud-based online services face significant sub-second load fluctuations while needing to meet strict Service Level Objectives (SLOs). Cluster operators often over-provision resources to protect SLOs, sacrificing utilization and cost efficiency. Existing reactive and proactive autoscalers, serverless (FaaS) deployments, and VM/FaaS hybrid systems fail to reconcile strict SLO compliance with low cost and high utilization under fine-grained load fluctuation. We introduce Spandana, an architecture that addresses this trade off by decoupling SLO enforcement from cost optimization. A lightweight controller colocated with each application VM enforces SLOs by steering each arriving request between the VM and FaaS. Requests that can meet the SLO stay on the VM; the remaining requests are forwarded to a stock FaaS layer such as AWS Lambda. For cost optimization, Spandana's resource allocator determines the most-efficient VM provisioning by accounting for VM cost, FaaS cost, and traffic volatility, allowing the VM pool to run at high utilization. Our evaluation shows that Spandana maintains strict SLO adherence, achieves 76-86% CPU utilization, and reduces cost by 5-44% over three SOTA baselines.

papers.title: Approximating Minimum Dominating Set with Few Awake Rounds
papers.summary: We study the Minimum Dominating Set (MDS) problem in the sleeping CONGEST model (Chatterjee, Gmyr, and Pandurangan, PODC 2020), a generalization of the standard CONGEST model, in which a node may sleep in some rounds and can only compute, send messages, or receive messages when it is awake. The awake complexity of an algorithm in this model is the worst case number (over all inputs and all nodes) of rounds a node is awake for during the execution of the algorithm. While there are several $O(\log \Delta)$-approximation algorithms (in expectation) for MDS that run in $O(\log^2 \Delta)$ rounds, all of these have $\Omega(\log^2 \Delta)$ awake complexity. Whether this awake complexity can be improved is the question that drives our work. We present the first $O(\log \Delta)$-approximation algorithm for MDS with $O(\log \Delta)$ awake complexity. The approximation guarantee holds in expectation, and the algorithm runs in $O(\log^2\Delta)$ rounds. We can reduce the awake complexity further, but at the cost of approximation: we present, for any $1<\alpha\le\min\{\Delta,\log n\}$, an algorithm in the sleeping CONGEST model that computes an $\tilde{O}(\alpha\log_\alpha\Delta)$-approximate dominating set in expectation in $\tilde{O}(\log\Delta\cdot \log_{\alpha} \Delta)$ rounds with $\tilde{O}(\log_{\alpha} \Delta)$ awake complexity. Our results depend on a generalization of the CONGEST model Set Cover algorithm of Grunau, Mitrovi\'c, Rubinfeld, and Vakilian (SODA 2020) that we develop. This generalization computes an $O(p\cdot q\cdot\log_p\Delta)$-approximate dominating set in $O(\log_p\Delta\cdot\log_q\Delta)$ rounds for parameters $1<p,q\le\Delta$. Our sleeping CONGEST algorithms apply a variety of techniques including sampling-based estimation and scheduling using virtual binary trees to the aforementioned 2-parameter Set Cover algorithm.

papers.title: CIDERS: Cloud-Edge LLM Collaborative Learning via Accelerating Personalized Bilevel Optimization
papers.summary: Amid the rapid advancement of physical-world intelligence, cloud-edge collaborative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising roadmap for practical LLM deployment. However, existing cloud-edge paradigms struggle to balance global consensus with local personalization, which fails to satisfy the need for a unified knowledge foundation on the cloud and domain-specific adaptation at the edge. To address this, we introduce, for the first time, a personalized bilevel optimization framework that formalizes cloud-edge LLM collaboration as a dual structure: the upper level optimizes edge-side personalization, while the lower level governs cloud-side knowledge transfer, reaching cloud-edge evolving in coordination. We then propose CIDERS, an efficient solver that decomposes the model into a learnable backbone and a messenger. While the cloud performs knowledge transfer to the learnable backbone, the key lies in embedding global trajectories into each local personalization step via consensus-variate correction to reconcile personalization with consensus. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including a geometric characterization of the local trajectory and a full convergence guarantee, revealing an explicit trade-off structure between personalization and global convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CIDERS consistently outperforms competitive baselines on the compressed edge path, with 3.1x and 1.7x gains on mathematical reasoning and code generation, respectively, and a 10\% relative gain on instruction metrics. Mechanism experiments attribute these gains to early consensus-corrected coordination and task-aware distillation. Overall, CIDERS offers a viable path toward consensus-guided continuous personalization in cloud-edge LLM systems.

papers.title: MpFA: Hardware-Efficient Train-Free QK4V8 FlashAttention Kernels on Blackwell GPUs
papers.summary: Long-context LLM inference pushes modern GPU serving stacks into an attention-bound regime, where both compute and memory are dominated by the softmax-GEMM pipeline. On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, FP4 Tensor Cores offer high matmul throughput, but we find that fully FP4 attention often fails to translate this throughput into end-to-end speedups due to non-matmul costs: online quantization after softmax, tensor/shared-memory data movement, and contention on the softmax path. We present MpFA, a training-free FlashAttention kernel optimized for Blackwell. Guided by hardware characterization, MpFA uses mixed precision: NVFP4 for QK and FP8 for PV (QK4PV8). This preserves low-bit QK throughput while avoiding the conversion and scaling overheads of FP4 PV. To recover accuracy without further stressing the softmax pipeline, MpFA introduces rank-one smoothing compensation implemented as an additional Tensor Core MMA. MpFA further improves performance with a fine-grained asynchronous pipeline, tensor-memory reuse, and adaptive parallel partitioning across prefill and decode. On an NVIDIA SM100 GPU and across 16K-128K contexts, MpFA improves prefill throughput over state-of-the-art BF16/FP8 baselines and increases end-to-end output throughput by 2.81$\times$ over BF16 FA4 across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B. Across five benchmark suites and two models, rank-one compensation recovers 62.5% of the accuracy loss with about 2.0% kernel overhead.

papers.title: Distributed Hybrid Quantum-Classical Optimization for Robust AoII Minimization in Satellite-Ground Integrated Edge Networks
papers.summary: Edge servers acting on monitored processes need estimates that are correct, not just recent. In satellite-ground integrated networks (SGINs), handover and shadowing interrupt links long enough for the process to change state several times, motivating the age of incorrect information (AoII). We formulate VANGUARD, a robust problem that jointly sets update rates, association, and bandwidth to minimize the worst-case AoII across disruption scenarios, and we solve it with SENTINEL, a distributed hybrid quantum-classical procedure. A renewal-interval decomposition yields a closed-form cost per delivery interval for AoII. The minimax is dualized into classically updated scenario weights, so each domain solves a linear assignment encoded as a compact quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem with XY-mixer-enforced one-hot constraints; domains are coordinated by the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and every schedule is certified by its exact worst-case AoII. Under Starlink passes and the 3GPP TR 38.811 channel, the certificate held in 98.7\% of epochs, and the robust one was 2 to 7\% below the nominal one at no cost in realized AoII. The compact encoding uses four to six times fewer qubits than an epigraph encoding; thirteen domains, each 8 to 38 qubits, run on IBM Heron processors and are decoded to the exact optimum.

papers.title: CACHEFORGE: LLM-Guided End-to-End Generative Cache Replacement Policy for Performance and Hardware Efficiency
papers.summary: Modern cache replacement designs saturate because they operate within fixed representational structures, hand-crafted and heuristic based feature-engineered predictors, or offline imitation models that cannot generate new decision logic on their own. At the same time, replacement is shaped by the causal interaction of prefetching, thrashing, spatial locality, and access-type behavior, producing an enormous design space that is difficult to traverse manually. Prior approaches typically rely on heuristics, parameter tuning, or imitation of an offline optimal policy, capturing correlations rather than synthesizing new mechanisms. As a result, their performance gains often plateau and they overfit under dynamic workload conditions. CACHEFORGE is the first framework to evolve cache-replacement policies end-to-end by embedding a large language model inside a governed hardware-aware loop. In each iteration, the LLM proposes new C++ replacement logic, the policy is evaluated under a trace-based CRC-2 ChampSim simulator, and the framework enforces feasibility through reward shaping, structural checks, dynamic mutation, temperature scheduling, and cross-policy crossover. This closed-loop generation-evolution loop specifically designed for cache replacement policy enables the discovery of compact policies that satisfy hardware constraints while exploring algorithmic transformations beyond fixed predictor structures. Across SPEC CPU2006, CACHEFORGE outperforms all CRC-2 baselines. It improves the total hit rate by 27.36%, 19.69%, 13.72%, 13.15%, 11.83%, and 5.73% over MPPPB, ReD, Hawk-eye, SHiP++, LIME, and LRU, respectively. On memory-intensive workloads, it increases IPC by 10.15%, 7.89%, 6.34%, 3.64%, 3.12%, and 2.71% over LRU, MPPPB, LIME, ReD, SHiP++, and Hawkeye.

papers.title: AgentWeave: Efficient Distributed Agent Serving via Flow Decomposition
papers.summary: Agent applications are evolving into workflows composed of large language model (LLM) calls and tool invocations, termed modules. Existing distributed agent systems typically adopt a disaggregated architecture, deploying different modules on separate devices. While this enables pipeline parallelism, imbalanced module latencies introduce severe pipeline bubbles that limit throughput. A natural alternative is an aggregated architecture that co-deploys all modules across all devices, eliminating bubbles by keeping every device continuously active. However, this introduces request blocking: short requests are forced to progress in lockstep with longer ones in the same batch, and newly arriving requests must wait until the entire ongoing batch completes the full workflow. To address this, we propose AgentWeave, an efficient distributed serving system for agent applications built on the aggregated architecture. Its core mechanism, flow decomposition, decomposes long agent requests into fine-grained execution units while preserving agent semantics, allowing short and newly arriving requests to proceed without being stalled by long-running ones. Complementing this, a flow-adaptive scheduler dynamically balances the throughput gains of decomposition against its scheduling overhead. Experiments across four representative agent applications demonstrate that AgentWeave improves throughput by 1.28-1.81x, reduces average latency by 2.08-2.45x, and reduces P90 latency by 1.56-2.04x over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Packet Interval Modulation for Uncoordinated NFC Data Networking Around Meander E-Textiles
papers.summary: Smart home sensing with low-power wireless nodes is non-intrusive but requires battery maintenance and cannot identify residents. A garment with a meander-coil NFC reader solves both, as it powers battery-free tags on the skin and on nearby objects and attributes every reading to its wearer. Because the number of tags in range changes as the user moves, we propose packet interval modulation (PIM), which encodes sensor values into pulse intervals without reader commands. With five tags, PIM reduces the collision rate of slotted ALOHA from 22.7% to 4.1% while delivering 384 bps, enabling resident-attributed ambient sensing.

papers.title: Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence
papers.summary: This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi's computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines. Well-known heuristic techniques for obtaining weakest preconditions are shown to be expressible in categorical terms and are proved sound. The ``baking in the frame rule'' trick is shown to satisfy a universal property. Constructions are given for extending a program logic with cost credits. Our largest case study is parametrized by a category having local independent product (LIP) structure, a notion due to Simpson that axiomatizes name generation, randomness, and local state. From an LIP category, we construct an allocation monad, a bunched fibration, and a monad lifting. We instantiate our construction to obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that both simplifies and clarifies prior work.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-ased Management of Continuum Resources
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

papers.title: Holonic Graceful Transitions Across Centralized, Decentralized, Distributed, and Local Control in DER-rich Cyber-Power Distribution System
papers.summary: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) in distribution system necessitates adaptive coordination frameworks. These frameworks must remain optimal during normal operation and resilient under cyber physical disturbances. Existing coordinated control approaches are typically deployed as static architectures with limited ability to adapt when communication degrades, local instability emerges, and operating conditions become spatially heterogeneous. This work addresses the gap by proposing a DER service-independent edge autonomous holonic adaptive coordination framework. In this framework, each DER controller executes its own control actions and transitions among centralized, distributed, decentralized, and local autonomous coordination modes without always relying on static coordination commands from the grid operator. The framework preserves coordination continuity across modes by retaining local controller states while reconfiguring only the coordination topology, information exchange pattern, and fallback action associated with the active DER service. Graceful transitions are enabled through dwell timers, rate limiting, and safety overrides to prevent dynamic instability during mode changes. Volt VAR control is used as a representative distribution automation application to validate the proposed architecture in a cyber-physical Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed. The proposed approach is evaluated under diverse cyber-physical event-based scenarios, showing region-confined adaptation under localized disturbance, reduced coordination traffic during coordination switching, and node-confined mitigation under cyber attack through edge anomaly detection and neighbor-corroborated impact estimation.

papers.title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
papers.summary: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.
